subject: Latent Spatial Field and Covariates Occuring on a Lattice

messages.author: eb8f81cb4d55140d
messages.subject: Latent Spatial Field and Covariates Occuring on a Lattice
parts:
Hello,

I am working with a spatial data set where the covariates and the gaussian latent field (under my assumptions) occur on a chessboard-like lattice. So for square i = 1,..,N, we have 

x_i = \beta_0 + F_i\beta + u_i

where F_i are the covariates for the ith square, \beta is a vector of linear coefficients and u_i is the realization of the discrete gaussian process, where u ~ N(0, Q^{-1}) and Q^{-1} is generated by a Matern covariance function.

Observations of the response, y_j, j=1,..,n, occur on the resolution of circles laid over the square grid. I assume the response is a weighted average of the intersecting squares with weights proportional to the area of overlap of each square.

y_j = A_j x + \epsilon_j

or possibly

y_j ~ f(y_j | \mu_j =  A_j x)

where A_j is a N length row vector of mostly zeros summing to one. The goal is the posterior distributions of x_i | y.

All of this reminded me very much of the SPDE-INLA approach, except my "mesh" is provided to me by the form of the data and my projector matrix A I can construct myself as described previously. I read through some of the SPDE tutorials, but am still unsure of how to implement this in R-INLA. Many of the 'inla.spde' functions seem to take a mesh as an input, when I am by bypassing this step. Additionally, I'll need to incorporate my own buffer zone to avoid boundary effects, which I am unsure how to do.

Any advice or examples somebody can point me to?

Thanks,
Paul

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Latent Spatial Field and Covariates Occuring on a Lattice
parts:
Hi Paul,
it looks like the only "non-standard" aspect is that you're observing different linear combinations than in the usual examples that use point-referenced observations.
You can in principle link that to exactly the same underlying latent model. On the lattice, you have two main options: one is to use the matern2d model that constructs a GMRF version of a Matern model on a lattice,
or you build a mesh of the lattice (e.g. by giving the mesh points as input to inla.mesh.2d(), and then specify suitable extensions as usual).
The only step that would be different than for the usual spde models would be that you wouldn't call inla.spde.make.A() but instead your own "A-maker" method.

Finn
